content: There is an old story about a shepherd who counted his sheep at dusk and came up one short. He left the ninety nine safe in the fold and walked the dark hills calling one name. When he found the little lamb, he did not scold it. He carried it home on his shoulders. That is how Jesus comes looking for you.

Picture a lighthouse keeper climbing the winding stairs every evening to light the great lamp. He never meets most of the ships that pass in the night. He only keeps the light burning. Tonight, somewhere out on the dark water, someone is steering home by the light you keep. Keep it burning, friend.

Imagine a small boy who wakes in the night, frightened by the wind against the window. He pads down the hall and climbs into his father's lap. The wind does not stop, but the boy falls asleep anyway, because his father is near. Our Father is near tonight too, and He does not sleep.

Once there was a farmer whose fields lay dry all summer. His village gathered at the church to pray for rain. Only one little girl came carrying an umbrella. The farmer smiled at her, and then he understood. She was the only one who had come expecting God to answer. Pray tonight like the girl with the umbrella.

A tale is told of a grandmother who made a quilt from scraps: a piece of a wedding dress, a patch from a work shirt, a square from a baby blanket. Alone, each scrap looked worn and plain. Sewn together, they made something warm and beautiful. God is stitching the pieces of your life together too.

Picture an old hymnal on a church pew, its pages soft and its spine cracked. Pencil marks fill the margins, dates beside favorite hymns, a name, a tear stain. Many hands have held it through weddings and funerals and ordinary Sundays. The book wore out, but the faithfulness it sang about never did.

Imagine a farmhouse on a lonely country road, with one lamp left burning in the front window all night. Travelers passing in the dark see it and feel a little less alone. Christ is the Light of the world, and His light is still burning in the window for every weary traveler tonight.

Once there was a night train rolling through the dark countryside. A child asked her mother how the engineer could see so far ahead. Her mother said he only needs to see as far as the headlight shines, and the track does the rest. God does not always show us the whole road, only the next stretch of track.

An old story tells of a potter at his wheel. A jar collapsed in his hands, and his apprentice expected him to throw the clay away. Instead the potter gathered it up, wet it again, and began once more. God is like that potter. He does not throw us away when we fall apart. He shapes us again.

There once lived a woodcarver who kept a small block of cedar on his shelf for years. Neighbors asked why he never carved it. He said he was waiting to see what was inside. One winter he carved a shepherd holding a lamb. God sees what He is making in us long before anyone else can.

Consider a seed buried in cold ground in the dead of winter. Nothing seems to be happening at all. Yet down in the dark, roots are quietly reaching. By spring a green shoot breaks the surface. Some of your best growing may be happening in the dark seasons, where only God can see.

Picture a mother bird gathering her chicks under her wings as a storm rolls in. The thunder is loud, but under those wings it is warm and still. The psalmist said we can hide under the shadow of God's wings. That is a fine place to fall asleep tonight.

Imagine a little girl learning to swim. She is afraid to let go of the side of the pool, until her father stands in the water and says, I am right here. She lets go and floats. Faith is a lot like that. We let go of the side because the One who holds us is close.

Long ago, so the story goes, a king left a single candle burning in a vast dark hall. A servant asked how one small flame could matter in so much darkness. The king said, look closer. The darkness had not swallowed the candle. The candle had pushed back the darkness. A little light goes a long way.

A gentle story is told of an old clockmaker who wound every clock in his shop before bed. One night his grandson asked if the clocks ever stopped while he slept. He said no, child, I wound them. God has wound the stars and set the morning in its place. You can sleep. He has it in hand.

Think of a weaver working on a tapestry from the back side. All she sees are knots and loose threads and tangled colors. But the master on the other side sees the pattern. Some nights our lives look like the back of the tapestry. God sees the front, and He is making something beautiful.

Once upon a winter night, a traveler lost his way in the snow. He saw a faint light and followed it to a small cabin, where an old man opened the door and said, we have been expecting someone. There was soup on the stove and a bed made up. Jesus said He goes to prepare a place for us. The door will be open.

There is a story about a little boat tied to a dock during a storm. The waves tossed it up and down all night, but it did not drift away, because it was tied fast. The boat could not hold the dock. The dock held the boat. Your hope is anchored in Christ, and He holds on to you.

Picture yourself on a front porch late on a summer night, the crickets singing and the stars coming out one by one. The same God who named every one of those stars knows your name too. He is not too busy with the universe to listen to you tonight.

Recall a father teaching his son to ride a bicycle. He runs alongside, one hand on the seat. The boy pedals faster and faster and shouts, I am doing it all by myself. He does not know his father is still holding on. Some nights we feel alone, but our Father's hand has never let go.

There is an old story about a man who carried a heavy sack of stones up a hill every day, believing he had to. One day a stranger asked him why. The man had no answer. The stranger said, set them down. Jesus said, come to Me, all who are weary and heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

A tale is told of a mountain village where the church bell rang every evening at sundown. Farmers in the fields would stop and bow their heads. No one rushed. The bell simply reminded them the day belonged to God. Let this hour of the night be your evening bell, a reminder to rest in Him.

Once there was a lamp maker who sold lamps that would not light, because no one had filled them with oil. A wise woman came and filled hers before dark. When night fell, her house glowed. Jesus told a story of lamps and oil and readiness. Keep your heart filled with Him, and the night will not catch you unready.

An old parable describes two houses built side by side. One on sand, one on rock. On sunny days you could not tell them apart. Then came the storm. Only the house on the rock was still standing in the morning. Whatever storm is blowing tonight, stand on the Rock. He will hold.

Picture a night nurse walking softly down a hospital hallway at three in the morning, checking on each patient by the glow of a small light. She does not wake them. She simply watches over them. The Bible says the One who keeps you will not slumber. He is making rounds tonight too.

Somewhere tonight, imagine a trucker on a long empty highway in the middle of the night. The radio is low, the coffee is cold, and the miles roll on. Then he sees the lights of a truck stop, warm and bright. Rest is ahead. For every weary pilgrim, there is a place of rest ahead, and the Lord is already there.

Think about a sparrow sitting on a fence in winter. It has no barn, no pantry, no savings. Yet it finds enough each day. Jesus pointed to birds like that and said, your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they? Tonight, let that little sparrow preach you a sermon on worry.

One tale tells of an old violin left in an attic for years, dusty and out of tune. A musician found it, restrung it, and played a hymn so sweet the whole house went quiet. Nobody had known what was in that old violin. In the Master's hands, nothing and no one is beyond use.

There once lived a shepherd boy who sang to his sheep at night so they would know he was near. When wolves howled in the hills, the sheep did not run. They heard his voice and stayed close. Jesus said My sheep hear My voice. Listen tonight. He is singing over you.

Consider the lilies in a field. They do not hurry. They do not fret about tomorrow. They simply grow where they are planted, turned toward the sun, and they are dressed more beautifully than any king. Jesus said, if God so clothes the grass of the field, will He not much more clothe you?

See in your mind a small country church on a snowy Christmas Eve, candles in every window and the old pump organ wheezing out Silent Night. Outside the snow falls soft. Inside, farmers and widows and children sing together. The same Savior who came to Bethlehem comes gladly to small places still.

A story is told of a little girl who asked her grandfather why he prayed every night when he was so old and had prayed so many times already. He said, sweetheart, I do not pray because I am running out of time. I pray because I am running toward Someone I love.

Sailors tell of a ship at sea in the fog, its captain listening for the sound of a bell buoy. He cannot see the harbor, but he can hear the bell and steer toward it. Some nights we cannot see the way. But we can still hear the Word of God ringing out, and we can steer by it.

Once upon a time, a child planted an acorn in a pot and watered it every day. Nothing came up for weeks, and she nearly gave up. Then one morning a tiny green leaf appeared. Her mother said, the acorn was busy all along, you just could not see it. God is busy in your life even when nothing seems to change.

An old illustration speaks of a man crossing a frozen river. He crept along on his hands and knees, terrified the ice would break. Then a farmer drove a team of horses and a heavy wagon right past him, singing. The ice was just as strong for both of them. Our safety rests on the strength of Christ, not the strength of our faith.

Picture an old porch swing creaking slowly in the evening breeze. A grandmother sits there with her Bible open on her lap, reading by the last light of day. She has outlived many friends and many troubles, yet she is at peace. The Word that held her up will hold you up too.

Folks tell of a boy who got lost in a crowded fair. He stood still and cried until he heard his father call his name across the crowd. He knew that voice anywhere. The good Shepherd calls His own sheep by name. Be still tonight and listen. He knows yours.

Think of a stone tossed into a still pond at evening. The ripples spread out wider and wider until they touch the farthest shore. A kind word, a prayer, a meal carried to a neighbor, these are stones in the pond. God carries their ripples farther than you will ever see.

Imagine the village baker rising before dawn, kneading dough in a quiet kitchen while the town sleeps. By sunrise the whole street smells of fresh bread. Jesus called Himself the Bread of Life. While the world sleeps, He is already preparing what we will need for tomorrow.

A parable tells of a shepherd who built his sheepfold with only one gate, and at night he lay down across the opening himself. Nothing could get in or out without passing him. Jesus said, I am the door of the sheep. Tonight you are inside the fold, and He is lying across the doorway.

In a story I love, a widow set two cups on the table every morning, one for herself and one for the Lord. She talked with Him over coffee like an old friend. Her neighbors thought it odd. But she was never lonely a day in her life. He is the Friend who sticks closer than a brother.

Try to picture a miner deep underground when his lamp flickers out. In total darkness he stays put and waits, because he knows the others will come looking. Soon a beam of light swings around the corner. Christ came into our darkness looking for us. Stay put. Help is already on the way.

Suppose a man is given a beautiful gift, wrapped and tied with a bow, and he sets it on the shelf and never opens it. Years later he finds it still unopened. Grace can be like that. It has been given freely. Tonight would be a fine night to open it and say thank You.

There was once a gardener who pruned his grapevine hard every winter. His neighbor said, you are killing it. The gardener said, wait until summer. That summer the vine hung heavy with fruit. Jesus said the Father prunes the branches so they bear more fruit. Some cutting is really caring.

Imagine the candlelight service on Christmas Eve, and a child holding a candle. Her flame is lit from her neighbor's candle, and she turns to light the next one. Soon the whole dark room is glowing. That is how the gospel has traveled for two thousand years, one small flame lighting another.

A tale is told of a weary pilgrim walking toward a far city. Each evening he set up camp a little closer, and each night he could see its lights a little brighter. He did not mind the road so much, knowing where it led. We are pilgrims too, and every night brings us one day closer to home.

Close your eyes and picture a still lake at midnight, so calm it reflects every star overhead. When the water is troubled, it reflects nothing clearly. When it is quiet, it mirrors heaven. Be still, and know that He is God. A quiet heart reflects Him best.

A fisherman in an old story mended his nets every night by lantern light. A young man asked why he worked so late on nets that would only tear again. He said, a mended net is a hopeful net. God mends us the same way, night after night, because He has not given up hope on us.

Think of a mother rocking her newborn at two in the morning, humming the only lullaby she can remember. She is tired beyond words, but she would not trade this moment. The Lord says a mother may forget her nursing child, yet I will not forget you. His love is even more tender than hers.

Grandfathers used to tell of a bridge builder who was asked why he built a bridge he would never cross himself. He said, there is a child coming behind me who will need it. Every prayer you pray, every kindness you sow, is a bridge for someone coming behind you.

Picture an old barn on a hill, its red paint faded, its roof patched many times. It has sheltered cattle through blizzards for a hundred winters. It is not fancy, but it is faithful. God loves faithful things. A faithful heart that keeps showing up is beautiful to Him.

Imagine an orchestra tuning up before a concert, every instrument making its own noise. It sounds like confusion. Then the conductor lifts his baton, and everything comes together in harmony. Life can feel like the tuning up. But our God is the conductor, and the music is coming.

Long ago, the story goes, a little village kept a watchman on the wall all through the night. Every hour he called out, all is well. The people slept soundly because someone was watching. The psalm says, except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh in vain. The Lord is keeping watch tonight.

A simple tale tells of a boy who carried a small lantern through the woods at night. He was afraid he could only see a few steps ahead. His grandfather said, son, a few steps is all you need. Keep walking and the light walks with you. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet.

The tale of a carpenter goes like this. He made a chair for a little child, sanding every edge smooth so it would not leave a splinter. He worked late into the night to finish it. Our Savior was a carpenter too, and He takes that same care with every soul He shapes.

Suppose you are carrying a heavy bucket of water up a long hill, and a stranger walks up and takes the other handle. Suddenly the load is half as heavy. That is what Jesus meant when He said, take My yoke upon you. He does not hand you the load and leave. He carries it with you.

Call to mind a country doctor driving through a snowstorm at midnight to sit at a sick child's bedside. He does not complain about the hour. He only asks, how is she breathing. Jesus is the Great Physician, and there is no hour too late and no road too long for Him to come.

There once was an old man who planted a pecan tree at the age of eighty. His neighbors laughed and said he would never taste a single pecan. He said, my grandchildren will. Faith plants for a future it may not see. Hebrews says the saints of old saw the promises from afar and embraced them.

Remember the snow globe on the windowsill at Grandmother's house. Shake it, and the whole little village disappears in a blizzard. Set it down and wait, and the snow settles, and the village appears again, peaceful as ever. When life is shaken, be still a while. Let it settle. God has not gone anywhere.

A fable tells of a little candle that was afraid of the dark night. A wise old lamp said, little one, the dark is the reason you were made. Without the night, no one would need you. Jesus said, you are the light of the world. Your light matters most where it is darkest.

Many a mother leaves the porch light on until every child is home. Even when they are grown and gone, she still leaves it on some nights, just in case. The father of the prodigal was watching the road. Our heavenly Father still leaves the light on for every child.

A girl in a story I heard kept a jar by her bed and dropped in a note every time God answered a prayer. On hard nights, she would pour them out and read them by flashlight. Remembering what God has done gives us courage for what we are facing now.

Sea stories tell of a sailor caught in a storm who lashed himself to the mast so the waves could not wash him overboard. The ship pitched and rolled all night, but he held fast. By morning the sea was calm. When the storms of life come, bind yourself to Christ. He will see you through to morning.

Somewhere in an old village square stands a stone well. For hundreds of years, every generation has drawn water from it. The bucket changes, the rope wears out, but the spring underneath never runs dry. Jesus offers living water, and the spring of His love has never run dry.

Imagine an old man sitting by a fireplace on a winter night, adding one log at a time. He does not pile them all on at once. He just keeps the fire going. Faith is often like that. Not one great blaze, but small faithful acts, one log at a time, all through the long night.

Here is a little story about a child who drew a picture for her father, all scribbles and crooked lines. He hung it on the refrigerator as if it were a masterpiece. Our offerings to God are often crooked and small. But He receives them with joy, because He loves the one who brings them.

Consider a young tree planted beside a river. When summer droughts come, the other trees wither, but this one stays green, because its roots go down to the water. The first psalm says the one who delights in God's word is like that tree. Send your roots down deep tonight.

Once upon a cold night, a stray puppy curled up on a doorstep. A little boy opened the door, picked him up, and carried him inside to the warm stove. The puppy had done nothing to earn it. That is grace. We were the ones on the doorstep, and Christ carried us in.

Let me paint you a picture. A tired mother finally sits down at the end of the day, and her toddler climbs up, lays his head on her chest, and falls asleep listening to her heartbeat. Rest like that tonight, with your head on the heart of God. You can hear it if you are still.

Envision a sheepdog lying at the edge of the meadow, half asleep but with one ear always listening. The sheep graze without fear. Goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, says the psalm. Like faithful sheepdogs, God's goodness and mercy are keeping watch behind you.

Jesus once told a parable of a king who made a wedding feast for his son. The invited guests made light of it and went their ways. So the king sent his servants out to the highways to gather everyone they found, and the wedding hall was filled. There is a seat at God's table with your name on it.

Say a jigsaw puzzle is spilled out on a kitchen table, a thousand pieces and no picture on the box. It seems hopeless. But the One who made the puzzle knows what every piece is for. Your life may feel like loose pieces tonight. The Maker knows the picture, and He is putting it together.

Years ago, in an old city, a lamplighter walked the streets at dusk lighting each lamp. You could watch his progress by the trail of lights he left behind. He himself disappeared into the dark, but the lights remained. May our lives leave a trail of light that points to Jesus.

Suppose a child is frightened by a thunderstorm and asks her father to stay until she falls asleep. He sits in the chair by her bed and holds her hand. She does not need the storm to stop. She only needs him to stay. And Jesus promised, I am with you always.

A mapmaker in an old story spent his life charting rivers and mountains. Near the end he said he had seen beautiful places, but he was most excited about the one place he had never seen. The Bible says eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what God has prepared for those who love Him.

The story is told of a widower who kept tending his late wife's rose garden. He was not much of a gardener, but every summer the roses bloomed anyway. He said, it is like she is still saying good morning. Love planted in God outlasts us. In Christ, every goodbye is only goodnight.

Let your mind drift to a small fishing boat setting out before dawn, its lantern swaying on the dark water. The fishermen do not know what the day will bring. But they go out anyway, trusting there are fish in the sea. Faith pushes off from shore each morning, trusting the Lord of the sea.

A gentle tale is told of an old woman who could no longer read her Bible because her eyes had failed. So she simply held it in her lap each night and said, Lord, You know what is in here, and You know what is in me. That was her prayer. And it was enough. God hears the prayers we cannot put into words.

In a quiet house at night, every light is switched off except a small nightlight in the hallway. It is not bright, but it is enough to keep a child from stumbling. Sometimes God gives us just enough light to take the next step. And just enough is plenty.

A little brook, the fable says, wondered if it mattered at all, being so small. It kept running anyway, down the hill, into a stream, into a river, into the sea. Your small faithfulness tonight flows into something bigger than you can imagine.

Someone once told of a man who could not sleep, so he decided to count his blessings instead of sheep. He started with the breath in his lungs and the roof over his head. By the time he reached his friends and family, he was smiling. He fell asleep somewhere around the mercy of God.

Above a sleeping town, imagine an old church steeple, its cross catching the moonlight. People pass beneath it every day without looking up. But it keeps pointing. It never stops pointing upward. May our lives point upward like that, quiet and steady, to the Savior.

Recall a little girl on a long car ride at night, falling asleep in the back seat. She does not watch the road or read the map. She trusts her father to drive. And when she wakes up, she is home, carried in from the car to her own bed. That is how the Lord will bring His children home.

A story is told of two brothers who farmed side by side. Each secretly carried sacks of grain to the other's barn at night, thinking his brother needed it more. One night they met on the hill between their farms, arms full, and embraced. Love that gives in secret is close to the heart of God.

Let us imagine a seashell held up to the ear. You hear the faint roar of the ocean, though you may be a thousand miles from the shore. God has set eternity in our hearts, the Bible says. That longing you feel at night for something more is the faint sound of home.

On a starry night, the story goes, a little girl asked her mother how many stars there were. Her mother said, more than anyone can count, but God counts them and calls each one by name. The girl thought for a moment and said, then He will not forget me. That is right, sweetheart. He will never forget you.

There was once a traveler who came to a fork in the road at night with no signpost. He knelt and prayed, then waited. Before long, the moon rose and lit the path to the right. Not every answer comes instantly, but the Lord does guide those who wait on Him.

Think about a father who keeps a photograph of his child in his wallet, worn soft from being pulled out so often. He shows it to anyone who will look. Did you know the Lord says, I have engraved you on the palms of My hands? You are that precious to Him.

Dream for a moment of a hiker reaching a mountain cabin after a long, cold day on the trail. There is a woodpile by the door and a note that says, rest here, friend. Someone thought of him before he arrived. Our Savior has gone ahead of us and left the light on and the door unlocked.

Kings in old tales sometimes disguised themselves as poor men to walk among their people and learn their troubles. Christ did far more than that. He did not merely visit. He became one of us, walked our dusty roads, and carried our sorrows all the way to the cross.

Children know the joy of a jar of fireflies on a summer evening, glowing softly on a nightstand. Each little light flickers on and off, yet together they light the room. The church is like that. None of us shine perfectly, but together we give light in a dark world.

A little boy in an old story broke his mother's favorite teacup and hid the pieces in shame. That night he confessed through tears. She held him and said, I love you far more than any teacup. Our heavenly Father is like that. Bring Him the broken pieces. He loves you more than you fear.

The tale of an old church organist is a sweet one. He practiced alone in the dark sanctuary every Saturday night. No one heard him but God. He said, the Sunday music is for the people. The Saturday music is for the Lord. Some of our sweetest worship happens when nobody else is listening.

Suppose you are lying awake listening to rain on a tin roof. It sounds like a thousand tiny drums, steady and soothing. Each drop waters a field somewhere. The prophet Isaiah said God's word is like the rain that comes down from heaven and does not return empty. Let it fall on your heart tonight.

Village lore tells of a bell that cracked and could no longer ring. The town hung it in the square anyway, as a reminder of all the weddings and Sundays it had rung for. Even when we feel cracked and quiet, God remembers every song our lives have sung for Him.

Here is a gentle picture. A baby sleeps in a cradle while her father builds a fire in the stove. She knows nothing of the cold outside. She only knows she is warm. That is a picture of grace. While we slept, unaware, our Father was already working to keep us warm and safe.

In old days, the story goes, a ferryman rowed travelers across a wide river at night. He knew every current and every rock. The travelers could sit back and rest, because the crossing was in his hands. When we come at last to the river of death, the Lord Himself will row us across to the other side.

The tale of a woman who saved every letter her husband wrote while he was away is a tender one. When she missed him, she would read them again by lamplight. The Bible is a letter like that, from a Lover who has gone to prepare a place. Read His letter tonight. He is coming back.

Watch a sunflower in a garden turn its face to follow the sun across the sky. Even on cloudy days, it faces the light. Hebrews says, looking unto Jesus. Whatever the weather of your heart tonight, turn your face toward Him. He is still shining behind the clouds.

A gentle parable speaks of a little lamb that wandered and was caught in thorns. The shepherd did not leave it there. He cut it free, washed its wounds, and carried it close. The marks of the thorns faded, but the lamb never again strayed far from the shepherd's side.

Think about a railroad switchman standing in the cold at night, waiting to turn the lever that sends a train safely onto the right track. The passengers never see him. They just arrive home. Many of God's answers are like that switchman, quietly turning us onto the right track while we sleep.

My favorite little story is about a girl who wrote her worries on slips of paper and dropped them in a little box she called the God box. When she opened it months later, nearly every worry was gone, answered or forgotten. Cast all your care upon Him, Peter wrote, for He cares for you.

Imagine an old pair of work boots by the back door, mud dried on them from a long day in the fields. The farmer is asleep now, his work done. There is honor in honest labor and sweetness in rest. The Lord gives His beloved sleep, says the psalm. Kick off your boots, friend.

Mountain folk tell of a mother eagle who stirs up her nest when it is time for the eaglets to fly. When one tumbles, she swoops beneath it and catches it on her wings. Deuteronomy uses that very picture of God. When you are falling, His wings are already underneath you.

A soldier in a story, far from home, carried his mother's small Bible in his pack. On lonely nights he would open it to the place she had underlined. Fear thou not, for I am with thee. Those words crossed oceans with him. The Word of God goes wherever we go.

Let us imagine a little chapel in the woods with a sign on the door that says, always open. There is no preacher there tonight, no choir, only a candle and a quiet bench. Yet anyone who stops will find God there. The door to the throne of grace is always open too.

Consider a weathervane on a barn roof spinning wildly in a storm, while the barn below stands perfectly still. Our feelings are like that weathervane, turning with every wind. But our faith is built on Christ, the solid foundation. Let the feelings spin. The foundation holds.

Suppose a little boy is told his father will come for him after school. Other parents come and go, and the boy waits by the gate. He is not worried. He only says, my father said he would come. That is how we wait for the Lord, not anxious, simply trusting His word.

Preachers used to tell of a cobbler who mended shoes for poor families and never charged them. When asked how he could afford it, he said, the Lord has mended my soul for free. How could I charge for a shoe? Grace received becomes grace given.

Imagine standing on a dark beach at night, watching the tide come in. You cannot stop it or hurry it. It comes in its own time, as faithful as the moon. God's mercies are like that tide. They are new every morning, and they never fail to come in.

Early one frosty morning, as an old story tells it, a grandfather walked his granddaughter to the barn to milk the cow before sunrise. She asked why they had to get up so early. He said, so we can see the day being born. Every sunrise is God's way of saying, I am not finished yet.

A story is told of a choir director who stopped a rehearsal because one quiet voice in the back row was missing. Everyone else said they could not tell the difference. He said, I can. God notices when you are missing from the song. Your voice matters to Him.

Step into a cozy kitchen on a winter night, a kettle starting to whistle and a dog asleep by the stove. Simple things. Ordinary things. Yet every one of them is a gift from above. James says every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights.

Imagine with me a cabin in the mountains during a blizzard, snowed in for days. The family inside reads, prays, sings and sleeps, unhurried for once. Sometimes the Lord lets us be snowed in, not to trap us, but to give us rest. He makes me to lie down in green pastures.

Watch a young mother teaching her child to pray at bedtime. The child mumbles the words half asleep and drifts off before the amen. The mother smiles and finishes the prayer for her. When we are too tired to finish our prayers, the Spirit intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered.

On the coast, the story goes, an old ship's bell was salvaged from the sea and hung in a seaside church. Every Sunday it rang for worship. The sailors said, that bell went down with a ship and came up to call people to God. The Lord brings beautiful things up out of deep waters.

A little girl, so the tale goes, was afraid of her dark bedroom until her mother hung a small cross made of glow paint on the wall. Every night, when the lights went out, the cross glowed. The darkness, she said, makes it easier to see. The cross shines brightest in our darkest nights.

Desert stories tell of a hermit who was asked what he did all day in his little hut. He said, I sweep the floor, I pray, I bake my bread, and I listen. The visitor said, that is all? He smiled and said, it is enough when God is in it. Ordinary life is holy when He is near.

Listen in your mind to a grandfather clock in a quiet hallway, its pendulum swinging slowly back and forth. Tick, tock, all night long. Time feels heavy at three in the morning. But your times are in His hands, says the psalm. Every minute of this night is held by the One who made time.

Look at a candle melting a little at a time to give its light. It does not mind becoming smaller, because that is its purpose. John the Baptist said, He must increase, but I must decrease. There is great peace in letting Jesus be the light, while we simply burn for Him.

Close your eyes and imagine a hammock strung between two old oaks, swaying gently in a summer breeze. You lie back, and the hammock holds all your weight. You do not have to hold yourself up. That is faith. Lean your whole weight on Christ tonight. He will hold you.

There was once a gardener who planted bulbs in autumn, knowing they would lie buried all winter. Her grandson asked why she planted something she could not see. She said, I am planting for spring. Every burial of a believer is like that. It is a planting, and spring is coming.

Picture, if you will, a mill by a river where the great wheel turned day and night. The miller slept soundly through it all, because the water never stopped flowing. God's grace is like that river. It keeps flowing while we sleep, turning the wheels of our lives.

Long ago, so the story goes, two travelers shared one blanket on a cold desert night. One said, it is too small for both of us. The other said, then let us move closer. The church is like that. When the night is cold, we draw near to one another, and it is enough.

Elijah stood on the mountain of God, worn out and afraid. A great wind tore at the rocks, but the Lord was not in the wind. Then an earthquake, then a fire, but the Lord was not in them. And after the fire came a still small voice. Sometimes God speaks loudest in the quiet of the night.

After a great victory, Elijah ran into the wilderness, lay down under a juniper tree, and asked to die. God did not scold him. An angel touched him and said, arise and eat. There was warm bread and a jar of water. Elijah slept again, then ate again. Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is rest.

When the brook Cherith was Elijah's only water, God sent ravens to bring him bread and meat, morning and evening. Ravens, of all creatures. God has unusual ways of delivering what we need, right on time, by the most unexpected messengers.

A widow in Zarephath had only a handful of flour and a little oil left. She was gathering sticks to bake one last meal. Elijah asked her to make him a small cake first. She trusted, and the flour barrel did not run empty and the oil jar did not run dry, day after day. God provides for those who trust Him.

Young Samuel was lying down in the temple at night, near the lamp of God, when he heard someone call his name. He ran to old Eli three times. Finally Eli understood and said, if He calls again, say, speak, Lord, for Thy servant heareth. Maybe tonight, in the quiet, the Lord is calling your name too.

Jacob was running from home, alone, with nothing but a stone for a pillow. That night he dreamed of a ladder reaching up to heaven, with angels going up and down. When he woke he said, surely the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not. God is nearer than you think, even on your loneliest night.

God took Abram outside one night and said, look up at the sky and count the stars, if you can. So shall your descendants be. Abram was old and had no child. But he believed the Lord, and it was counted to him as righteousness. Look up at the stars tonight. God still keeps His promises.

Gideon was unsure. So he laid a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and asked God to wet the fleece with dew and leave the ground dry. In the morning he wrung out a bowl of water. Then he asked for the opposite, and God did that too. The Lord was patient with a doubting man. He is patient with us too.

Ruth came softly to the threshing floor at night and lay down at the feet of Boaz. When he woke at midnight, startled, she asked him to spread his covering over her as her kinsman redeemer. Boaz blessed her kindness and promised to care for her. In Christ we have a Redeemer who covers us too.

Ruth, a young widow from Moab, went out to glean leftover grain. She happened to come to the field of Boaz. He noticed her and told his workers to drop extra handfuls on purpose. Happened, the Bible says. But it was no accident. God was quietly arranging her story, and He is arranging yours.

Under the cover of night, a Pharisee and ruler of the Jews named Nicodemus slipped in to talk with Jesus. In that quiet conversation, Jesus spoke of the wind and the Spirit, and then said the words we still treasure. For God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten Son. Those words were first spoken at night, to one honest seeker. Bring Him your questions tonight.

Shepherds were keeping watch over their flock by night outside Bethlehem, an ordinary shift like any other. Then the glory of the Lord shone around them, and an angel said, fear not, for behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy. The best news in history was first given to the night shift.

After the angels left, the shepherds said, let us go now to Bethlehem. They found Mary and Joseph and the baby lying in a manger, just as they had been told. They went back to their fields glorifying God. And Mary kept all these things and pondered them in her heart. Ponder them with her tonight.

Paul and Silas sat in the inner prison with their feet in stocks, their backs aching. At midnight they prayed and sang hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening. If you are singing in the dark tonight, someone may be listening, and God certainly is.

One evening Jesus said to His disciples, let us go over to the other side. A great storm arose, and the boat began to fill with water. And Jesus was in the back, asleep on a cushion. They woke Him, and He said to the sea, peace, be still. And there was a great calm. He can still speak peace to your storm.

Two sad disciples walked toward Emmaus at evening, talking about the cross. A stranger joined them and opened the Scriptures to them. At supper, when He broke the bread, their eyes were opened. It was Jesus. They said, did not our hearts burn within us. He walks beside us even when we do not recognize Him.

The disciples fished all night on the Sea of Galilee and caught nothing. At daybreak a man on the shore told them to cast the net on the right side, and the net filled. It was the Lord. When they came ashore, He had a charcoal fire going, with fish and bread. Jesus said, come and have breakfast.

Late in the night, the disciples were rowing hard against the wind on the lake. Then they saw Jesus walking toward them on the water. They were afraid, but He said, be of good cheer, it is I, be not afraid. When the night is long and the wind is against you, He still comes across the water to you.

Peter stepped out of the boat and walked on the water toward Jesus. But when he saw the wind, he was afraid and began to sink. He cried, Lord, save me. And immediately Jesus stretched out His hand and caught him. One short prayer was enough. If you are sinking tonight, that prayer is enough for you too.

Before Jesus chose His twelve disciples, He went out to a mountain to pray, and He continued all night in prayer to God. If the Son of God spent the whole night talking with the Father, then a sleepless night spent in prayer is not wasted. It may be the most important part of your day.

Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went out to a solitary place to pray. The crowds would come soon enough. But first, quiet time with His Father. Before the noise of tomorrow begins, you can meet Him in the stillness of these early hours.

In the garden of Gethsemane, on the darkest night of His life, Jesus prayed, not My will, but Thine, be done. Luke tells us an angel came from heaven and strengthened Him. If you are facing your own garden night, know that He has been there, and He understands.

King Herod had Peter chained between two soldiers, the night before his trial. And Peter was sound asleep. An angel had to strike him on the side to wake him. The chains fell off, and the gates opened by themselves. Peter could sleep because he trusted God. You can too.

When Peter, freed from prison, knocked at the door of the house where believers were praying, a girl named Rhoda heard his voice. She was so happy she forgot to open the door and ran to tell everyone. They said, you are out of your mind. God answered their prayer faster than they could believe it.

Daniel spent the night in the lions' den. The king could not eat or sleep, and at the first light of morning he ran to the den and called out. Daniel answered, my God has sent His angel and shut the lions' mouths. The king tossed all night. Daniel was the one at peace.

One night King Ahasuerus could not sleep, so he had the royal records read to him. He heard how Mordecai had once saved his life and had never been thanked. That sleepless night turned the whole story around for God's people. God can use even your sleepless nights for good.

Joseph was troubled, unsure what to do about Mary. While he thought on these things, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said, fear not to take Mary as your wife, for the child is of the Holy Spirit. Joseph woke up and obeyed. God can settle our troubled thoughts in the night.

An angel warned Joseph in a dream to take the child and His mother and flee to Egypt. Joseph got up and took them away by night. A quiet carpenter, obeying in the dark, protected the Savior of the world. Never underestimate a faithful heart that simply does the next right thing.

The wise men followed the star across the desert night after night. When it stopped over the place where the young child was, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy. They went in, saw the child with Mary His mother, and bowed and worshiped. Every star in tonight's sky still points to Him.

Old Simeon had waited his whole life to see the Messiah. One day Mary and Joseph brought the baby Jesus to the temple, and Simeon took Him in his arms and said, Lord, now lettest Thou Thy servant depart in peace, for mine eyes have seen Thy salvation. Waiting on God is never wasted.

Anna was a widow of about eighty four who never left the temple, but served God with fasting and prayer night and day. When she saw the baby Jesus, she gave thanks and spoke of Him to everyone. God has a special place for the older saints who keep praying through the night.

When Jesus was twelve, His parents lost track of Him on the way home from Jerusalem. After three days they found Him in the temple, listening and asking questions. He said, did you not know I must be about My Father's business. Even as a boy, His heart was at home with His Father.

When King Saul was troubled in spirit, young David would take his harp and play. And Saul was refreshed and was well. Music has always had a way of quieting a troubled heart. May the songs tonight do for you what David's harp did for Saul.

Samuel came to Jesse's house to anoint a king. One by one the tall, strong sons passed by, but God said no. The youngest, David, was out keeping the sheep. They had to send for him. God said, man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart. He sees your heart tonight.

David fled from his own son Absalom, heartbroken and in danger. Yet he wrote, I laid me down and slept, I awaked, for the Lord sustained me. On one of the worst nights of his life, David slept. Not because the trouble was gone, but because the Lord was holding him.

Jesus told of a shepherd with a hundred sheep who lost one. He left the ninety and nine and went after the lost one until he found it. Then he laid it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and called his friends to celebrate. There is joy in heaven over one who comes home.

Jesus told of a woman who lost one silver coin. She lit a lamp, swept the whole house, and searched carefully until she found it. Then she called her neighbors to rejoice. You are not lost in the dust to God. He lights the lamp and searches until He finds you.

A younger son wasted everything in a far country and came home hoping only to be a hired servant. But while he was still a great way off, his father saw him, ran to him, fell on his neck, and kissed him. Our Father runs to meet us. He is watching the road for you tonight.

A man was beaten and left half dead on the road to Jericho. A priest passed by, then a Levite. But a Samaritan stopped, bandaged his wounds, set him on his own animal, and paid for his care at an inn. Jesus said, go and do thou likewise. Kindness to the hurting is the heart of God.

Jesus said the kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground and then goes to sleep. Night and day the seed sprouts and grows, and he does not know how. You can go to sleep tonight. God is still growing what was planted. Growth does not depend on your worrying.

Jesus told of a man who knocked on his friend's door at midnight to borrow three loaves for an unexpected guest. The friend was already in bed, but because of the man's persistence, he got up and gave him what he needed. Jesus said, ask, and it shall be given you. Keep knocking, even at midnight.

Ten young women waited with lamps, Jesus said, for a bridegroom who came at midnight. Five had brought extra oil and five had not. The wise ones were ready when the cry went out, behold, the bridegroom cometh. Keep your lamp trimmed and your heart ready. He is coming.

Jesus said, behold the birds of the air. They do not sow or reap or gather into barns, yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Consider the lilies, how they grow. Therefore take no thought for tomorrow. Tomorrow has its own cares, and the Father already knows what you need.

Parents brought little children to Jesus, and the disciples tried to send them away. Jesus was displeased and said, suffer the little children to come unto Me. Then He took them up in His arms, put His hands on them, and blessed them. No one is too small for His arms.

Jairus's little daughter lay still, and the mourners said it was too late. Jesus took her by the hand and said, Talitha cumi, which means, little girl, I say to you, arise. She got up and walked. Then Jesus told them to give her something to eat. He cares for the big things and the small things.

Thousands were hungry on a hillside, and all anyone could find was a boy's lunch of five barley loaves and two small fish. Jesus gave thanks and fed the whole crowd, and twelve baskets were left over. Whatever little you have tonight, place it in His hands.

Martha was busy in the kitchen, worried about many things. Her sister Mary sat at Jesus' feet, listening. When Martha complained, Jesus said gently, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things, but one thing is needful. Tonight, let the dishes wait. Sit at His feet.

Mary of Bethany took a pound of costly ointment and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped them with her hair. John says the house was filled with the fragrance. Love that pours itself out for Jesus fills the whole house. Even a quiet act of devotion leaves a sweet aroma.

When Jesus came to the tomb of His friend Lazarus and saw Mary weeping, He groaned in His spirit, and Jesus wept. He knew He was about to raise Lazarus. He wept anyway. Our Savior does not hurry past our grief. He weeps with us, and then He brings life.

Mary stood weeping outside the empty tomb early in the morning, while it was still dark. She thought the man nearby was the gardener. Then He said one word, Mary. She knew His voice at once. The risen Lord still calls His sheep by name, even through our tears.

Thomas had not seen the risen Lord and said he would not believe unless he touched His wounds. Eight days later Jesus came and said, reach hither thy finger. Thomas answered, my Lord and my God. Jesus was gentle with his doubts. He is gentle with yours too.

As the disciples watched, Jesus was taken up, and a cloud received Him out of their sight. Two men in white said, this same Jesus shall so come in like manner as ye have seen Him go. He is not gone for good. He is coming back.

In a ship caught in a fierce storm for many days, with no sun or stars, Paul stood up and said, be of good cheer. An angel of God stood by me this night and said, fear not, Paul. He told them, I believe God. Every soul on board reached land safely. God stands by His own through the storm.

One night Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia pleading, come over into Macedonia and help us. Paul set out right away. God sometimes points the way in the night, and the gospel crossed into Europe because Paul listened.

In Corinth, when Paul may have been discouraged, the Lord spoke to him in the night by a vision. Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace, for I am with thee. Paul stayed there a year and six months. The Lord's night words can strengthen us for a long season.

After a hard day before the council, Paul was taken back to the barracks. The following night the Lord stood by him and said, be of good cheer, Paul. Whatever your day was like, the Lord can stand by you tonight with that same word. Be of good cheer.

Paul was preaching late into the night in an upstairs room lit by many lamps. A young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window, sank into a deep sleep and fell. Paul went down and embraced him, and the young man was brought back alive. If you nod off listening tonight, you are in good company.

Dorcas was known in Joppa for her good works, sewing coats and garments for the widows. When she died, the widows stood weeping, holding up the clothes she had made. Peter knelt and prayed, and God raised her up. A life of quiet kindness is never forgotten by God.

After the flood, God set His bow in the clouds and said, this is the token of the covenant. When I bring a cloud over the earth, the bow shall be seen in the cloud, and I will remember. Every rainbow is a reminder that God keeps His promises, even after the storm.

Noah sent a dove out from the ark, and in the evening she came back with an olive leaf in her beak, freshly plucked. Noah knew the waters were going down. Sometimes God sends a small sign in the evening that the flood is receding. Watch for the olive leaf.

Moses was tending sheep in the wilderness when he saw a bush burning but not burned up. When he turned aside to look, God called him by name and said, put off thy shoes, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground. God can meet you in an ordinary day, and make it holy.

A mother in Egypt hid her baby boy as long as she could, then placed him in a little basket of bulrushes among the reeds of the river. His sister watched from a distance. Pharaoh's own daughter found him and drew him out. God watched over that little basket, and He watches over your children too.

As Israel traveled through the wilderness, the Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light. He did not take away the pillar by day or the fire by night. God does not leave His people in the dark.

In the wilderness, every morning there was manna on the ground like frost, bread from heaven. They were to gather only enough for each day. Whatever was hoarded spoiled. God taught His people to trust Him one day at a time. Tomorrow's grace will come with tomorrow's sunrise.

During a battle, when Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed. But his arms grew heavy. So Aaron and Hur sat him on a stone and held up his hands, one on each side, until the going down of the sun. When you are weary, let others hold up your arms. And hold up theirs.

God gave Aaron a blessing to speak over His people. The Lord bless thee, and keep thee. The Lord make His face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee. The Lord lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace. Receive that blessing tonight as if it were spoken to you alone.

When Joshua took up the leadership after Moses died, the Lord told him, be strong and of a good courage, be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed, for the Lord thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest. New and frightening seasons come with the same promise. He goes with you.

King Hezekiah received a threatening letter from a powerful enemy. He went up to the house of the Lord and spread the letter out before the Lord, and prayed. God answered. Whatever letter, bill or bad report is weighing on you tonight, spread it out before the Lord.

Elisha's servant woke early to find an enemy army surrounding the city. He panicked. Elisha said, fear not, for they that be with us are more than they that be with them. Then he prayed, Lord, open his eyes. The hills were full of horses and chariots of fire. You are not as alone as you feel.

A woman in Shunem said to her husband, let us make a little room on the wall for the man of God, with a bed, a table, a stool and a candlestick. Elisha stayed there whenever he passed by. Simple hospitality, a lamp and a bed for a weary traveler, is precious in God's eyes.

A widow with debts had nothing in the house but a pot of oil. Elisha told her to borrow empty jars from all her neighbors, shut the door, and pour. The oil kept flowing until every jar was full. It stopped only when the jars ran out. Bring God your empty vessels. He is not short on oil.

From inside the great fish, in the deep dark, Jonah prayed. When my soul fainted within me I remembered the Lord, and my prayer came in unto Thee. No place is too deep and no darkness too thick for your prayer to reach the Lord.

Nehemiah came to ruined Jerusalem and went out by night with only a few men, quietly inspecting the broken walls. He told no one yet what God had put in his heart. Then he said, let us rise up and build. Some of God's best plans begin with a quiet walk in the night.

Mordecai said to Queen Esther, who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this. Esther asked her people to fast and pray, then she went to the king. God had placed her exactly where she was needed. He has placed you where you are for a reason too.

God answered Job out of the whirlwind and asked, where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth, when the morning stars sang together. Job did not get every answer. But he met the God who made the stars, and that was enough. Look up tonight. The One who made them is holding you.

At Gibeon the Lord appeared to young King Solomon in a dream by night and said, ask what I shall give thee. Solomon asked for an understanding heart to lead God's people. God was pleased and gave him wisdom, and more besides. You can bring your requests to Him in the night too.

Abraham's servant was sent to find a wife for Isaac. He stopped by a well at evening, when the women came to draw water, and prayed for guidance. Before he had finished praying, Rebekah came out with her pitcher on her shoulder. God sometimes answers before we finish asking.

Hagar ran away into the wilderness, alone and afraid. The angel of the Lord found her by a spring of water and spoke to her. She called the Lord, Thou God seest me. If you feel invisible tonight, the God who saw Hagar sees you.

Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide. He lifted up his eyes and saw the camels coming, bringing Rebekah to him. There is something good about walking quietly in the evening with God. He has a way of bringing answers into view.

Moses asked God, show me Thy glory. God said He would put Moses in a cleft of the rock and cover him with His hand while His glory passed by. Hidden in the rock, covered by God's own hand. That is where we are safe, in Christ, the Rock cleft for us.

Mephibosheth was lame in both feet, and he called himself a dead dog before King David. But David said, fear not, for I will surely show thee kindness for Jonathan thy father's sake. And he ate at the king's table continually, like one of the king's sons. That is grace. We are welcomed to the King's table.

David and Jonathan had to say goodbye in a field. They wept together, and Jonathan said, go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord. Faithful friendship is a gift from God. Thank Him tonight for the friends who have stood with you.

David came back to find his town burned and his family taken. His own men spoke of turning against him. The Bible says David was greatly distressed, but David encouraged himself in the Lord his God. When there is no one else to encourage you, the Lord Himself is your strength.

Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up, and the seraphim crying, holy, holy, holy. He cried, woe is me, for I am undone. An angel touched his lips with a coal and said, thy sin is purged. Then the Lord asked, whom shall I send. Isaiah said, here am I, send me. Grace always comes before the calling.

God sent Jeremiah down to the potter's house. The vessel the potter was making was marred in his hand, so he made it again into another vessel, as seemed good to him. God said, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in Mine. You are not ruined. You are being remade.

Three young men were thrown into a burning furnace for refusing to bow to an idol. The king looked in and said, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt. The Lord was in the fire with them. Whatever fire you face tonight, you do not face it alone.

When Daniel knew the decree had been signed against praying to anyone but the king, he went home, opened his windows toward Jerusalem, and knelt three times a day and prayed, as he had always done. A steady habit of prayer prepares us for the hardest days.

Zacharias was an old priest burning incense in the temple when an angel appeared and said, fear not, thy prayer is heard. His wife Elisabeth would have a son, John. They had prayed for years. Sometimes God answers a prayer we had long ago stopped expecting.

Mary hurried to the hill country to visit her cousin Elisabeth. When Elisabeth heard Mary's greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and she said, blessed art thou among women. Two expectant mothers, rejoicing together in God's promise. Faith grows when we share it.

The angel Gabriel came to a young girl in Nazareth named Mary and told her she would bear the Son of God. She asked how this could be. Gabriel said, with God nothing shall be impossible. Mary said, behold the handmaid of the Lord, be it unto me according to thy word.

Mary brought forth her firstborn son, wrapped Him in swaddling clothes, and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn. The King of glory slept in a feed trough among the animals. No place is too humble for Jesus to come.

When Jesus was baptized, the heavens opened and the Spirit of God descended like a dove and rested upon Him. A voice from heaven said, this is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. In Christ, the Father looks at you with that same love.

Peter had fished all night and caught nothing. Jesus said, launch out into the deep. Peter said, Master, we have toiled all the night, nevertheless at Thy word I will let down the net. The nets were so full they began to break. That word, nevertheless, can change a whole night.

On the night He was betrayed, Jesus rose from supper, laid aside His garments, took a towel, and washed His disciples' feet. The Lord of glory knelt with a basin of water. He said, I have given you an example. Greatness in God's kingdom looks like a towel and a basin.

At the Last Supper, with the night closing in, Jesus said, let not your heart be troubled. In My Father's house are many mansions. I go to prepare a place for you, and I will come again. He spoke peace to His friends on the darkest night. He speaks the same to you.

At evening, when the sun had set, they brought to Jesus all who were sick, and the whole city gathered at the door. And He healed many. The end of a long day did not stop His compassion. Evening is still a good time to bring your needs to His door.

The disciples came back from their work tired, with no time even to eat. Jesus said, come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while. The Lord who calls us to work also calls us to rest. Tonight, take Him up on the invitation.

Jesus watched people putting money into the temple treasury. Many rich people gave much. Then a poor widow dropped in two small coins. Jesus said she had given more than all of them, for she gave all she had. God measures our gifts by the heart, not the amount.

A Roman centurion asked Jesus to heal his servant, but said, Lord, I am not worthy that Thou shouldest come under my roof. Speak the word only. Jesus marveled at his faith, and the servant was healed in that same hour. One word from Jesus is enough.

Four friends carried a paralyzed man to see Jesus, but the house was packed. So they climbed onto the roof, opened it up, and let him down on his mat right in front of Jesus. Jesus saw their faith. Who are you carrying to Jesus in prayer tonight? Keep carrying them.

On the mountain, Peter, James and John saw Jesus transfigured, His face shining like the sun. They fell on their faces, terrified. Jesus came and touched them and said, arise, and be not afraid. When they lifted their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only. Jesus only, that is enough.

Saul of Tarsus had come to Damascus blind and shaken. The Lord told a disciple named Ananias to go to him. Ananias was afraid, but he went, laid his hands on him, and said, brother Saul. The first words Saul heard from a believer were words of welcome. Be an Ananias to someone.

When the believers in Jerusalem were afraid of the newly converted Saul, it was Barnabas who took him and brought him to the apostles and spoke up for him. Barnabas means son of encouragement. Every church needs a Barnabas, someone who believes in people before others do.

Paul wrote to young Timothy, I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice. A grandmother's faith passed down through a mother to a son. Your faith is a gift you can pass on.

John was an old man in exile on the island of Patmos when he saw the risen Christ in glory and fell at His feet as dead. Jesus laid His right hand on him and said, fear not, I am the first and the last. The glorified Christ still lays a gentle hand on His frightened servants.

In the city of God that John saw, there is no need of the sun or the moon, for the glory of God lightens it, and the Lamb is the light thereof. And there shall be no night there. For all who wait through long nights, a day is coming that will never end.

As the rooster crowed in the courtyard, the Lord turned and looked upon Peter, and Peter remembered His word, and went out and wept bitterly. That look was not anger. It was love. And after the resurrection, Jesus sent word especially to Peter. Failure is never the end with Jesus.

Before Peter's denial, Jesus told him, Simon, Satan hath desired to have you, but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not. Jesus prayed for Peter before he fell. Hebrews says He ever lives to make intercession for us. Tonight, Jesus is praying for you.

Paul begged God three times to take away his thorn in the flesh. God answered, My grace is sufficient for thee, for My strength is made perfect in weakness. Paul said, most gladly therefore will I glory in my infirmities. His grace is enough for whatever you carry tonight.

Paul wrote to the Philippians while in chains. Yet he said, rejoice in the Lord always, and again I say, rejoice. Be careful for nothing, and the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts. Peace written from a prison can keep your heart tonight.

Peter went up on a rooftop to pray around noon and fell into a trance. He saw a sheet let down from heaven, and God taught him that the gospel was for every nation. Prayer opened Peter's eyes to how wide God's love really is. It still does.

Moses was a baby in a basket, but by the end of his life he climbed Mount Nebo, and the Lord showed him all the promised land. Then Moses died there, and the Lord Himself buried him. God tends His faithful servants all the way to the end.

Elijah was taken up by a whirlwind into heaven as Elisha watched. Elisha picked up the mantle that fell from Elijah and went back to the Jordan. He struck the water and said, where is the Lord God of Elijah. The waters parted. The God of the old saints is our God still.

Jacob had his name changed after a long night of wrestling by the brook Jabbok. At daybreak he would not let go until he was blessed, and God gave him a new name, Israel. He walked away limping, but blessed. Some of God's best blessings come at the end of a long night.

On Palm Sunday Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey, and the crowds spread their garments in the way and cried, hosanna. When some asked Him to quiet them, He said, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out. All creation longs to praise Him.

The psalmist asked, whither shall I flee from Thy presence. If I say, surely the darkness shall cover me, even the night shall be light about me. The darkness and the light are both alike to Thee. Wherever you are at this hour, the night is not dark to God.

Boaz noticed the gleaner Ruth, and at mealtime he invited her to come and eat bread and dip her morsel. He handed her parched grain, and she ate until she was satisfied, with some left over. The Lord of the harvest invites the humble to His table.

The night before the crossing of the Red Sea, the pillar of cloud moved behind Israel. It was darkness to the Egyptians, but it gave light by night to Israel, and the Lord drove back the sea all that night with a strong east wind. God works through the night while His people wait.

On His last night with them, Jesus promised the disciples, I will not leave you comfortless, I will come to you. And He promised the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, to abide with them forever. You are not an orphan tonight. The Comforter is with you.

After the Last Supper, on the night before the cross, Jesus and His disciples sang a hymn, and then they went out into the night to the Mount of Olives. Our Lord sang on His way to Gethsemane. When you sing an old hymn at night, you are walking in His footsteps.

Peter's mother in law lay sick with a fever. Jesus came into the house, took her by the hand, and lifted her up. The fever left her at once, and she got up and served them. The Savior of the world took time for one sick woman in a small fishing town. He takes time for you.

As a young man in Southampton, Isaac Watts complained that the psalm singing at church was dull. According to a story often told about him, his father answered, then give us something better. Watts did, and went on to write hundreds of hymns. Sometimes a holy discontent is God's way of putting a song in your heart.

Isaac Watts based O God, Our Help in Ages Past on Psalm ninety and published it in seventeen nineteen. John Wesley later changed the first words from Our God to O God. For three centuries it has been sung at times of national grief and personal loss. Our shelter from the stormy blast, and our eternal home.
reference: O God, Our Help in Ages Past

content: In seventeen thirty six, young John Wesley sailed to Georgia. During a fierce Atlantic storm, a group of German Moravians calmly sang a psalm while the sea poured over the deck. Wesley asked one of them afterward if he had been afraid. He answered, I thank God, no. Wesley never forgot that peace in the storm.

Charles Wesley's Christmas hymn first began, Hark how all the welkin rings. George Whitefield changed it to Hark, the herald angels sing. The tune came later, adapted from a piece by Felix Mendelssohn, who said it would never do for sacred words. Today it is one of the best loved carols in the world.

In seventeen thirty nine George Whitefield preached in the open air to the coal miners of Kingswood, near Bristol. He wrote that he could see white gutters made by tears running down their blackened cheeks. The gospel was not only for fine churches. It reached men coming up from the dark pits.

Brother Lawrence was a humble lay brother who worked in a monastery kitchen in Paris in the sixteen hundreds. He learned to talk with God among the pots and pans, as easily as in prayer. His simple counsel, gathered after his death as The Practice of the Presence of God, still teaches us that God is near in ordinary work.

Patrick was taken from Britain as a teenager and made to tend flocks in Ireland. In his own Confession he wrote that he prayed as many as a hundred prayers in a day, and nearly as many at night, through snow and frost and rain. Years later he returned to Ireland as a missionary. God was with him on those lonely hills.

On a Sunday in June of eighteen sixty five, Hudson Taylor walked alone on the beach at Brighton, England, burdened for the millions of China. There on the sand he prayed for twenty four willing workers and surrendered the whole matter to God. Soon after, the China Inland Mission was born. Big works often begin with one quiet prayer.

George Muller cared for more than ten thousand orphans in Bristol, England, over his lifetime, and he made it his rule never to ask anyone but God for money. He kept careful journals of the prayers God answered. His life is a quiet witness that our heavenly Father knows how to provide.

In nineteen thirty one, missionary Amy Carmichael was injured in a fall in India, and she spent much of her last twenty years confined to her room. Yet from that little room she wrote books and letters that have strengthened believers ever since. God does not set aside His servants when their strength fails.

When Corrie ten Boom was a little girl, she asked her father how she could ever be strong enough to face hard things. He asked, when we take the train to Amsterdam, when do I give you your ticket? Just before we get on, she said. He said God gives us strength the same way, just when we need it, not before.

William Carey was an English shoemaker who kept a homemade map of the world on his wall while he worked. In seventeen ninety two he preached a sermon urging believers to expect great things from God, and attempt great things for God. The next year he sailed for India, where he spent the rest of his life.

In January of eighteen fifty six, facing danger in Africa, David Livingstone wrote in his journal about the words of Jesus, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. He wrote that it was the word of a gentleman of the most sacred honor, and that would be the end of it. He wrote that he felt quite calm.

In eighteen seventy four, Ira Sankey found a poem in a newspaper while riding a train in Scotland and tucked it away. At a meeting in Edinburgh, D. L. Moody unexpectedly asked him to sing. Sankey laid the clipping on his little organ and composed the tune as he sang. It became The Ninety and Nine.

One day in eighteen sixty eight, composer William Doane hurried to Fanny Crosby's room, played a new tune, and said he had only a short while before he had to catch a train. Fanny listened, and within minutes had the words for Safe in the Arms of Jesus. It became one of the most loved hymns of comfort in her lifetime.
reference: Safe in the Arms of Jesus

content: Fanny Crosby lost her sight as a baby, but she never blamed God. She said that if she could have had her sight, she would not have taken it, because the first face that would ever gladden her eyes would be the face of her Savior. What a beautiful way to wait for heaven.

At about eight years old, the blind girl who would become Fanny Crosby wrote her first little poem. She said, oh what a happy soul am I, although I cannot see, I am resolved that in this world contented I will be. A child's contentment grew into a lifetime of praise and thousands of hymns.

Fanny Crosby once needed five dollars and had no way to get it. As was her habit, she prayed. Soon a visitor pressed into her hand exactly five dollars. She said she had no way of accounting for it except that God had put it in his heart, and she wrote All the Way My Savior Leads Me. Robert Lowry set it to music.
reference: All the Way My Savior Leads Me

content: D. L. Moody often told an illustration about a ship trying to reach Cleveland harbor on a stormy night. The great lighthouse was shining, but the lower lights along the shore had gone out. Philip Bliss heard it and wrote Let the Lower Lights Be Burning. The Master keeps the great light. Our job is to keep the lower lights lit.
reference: Let the Lower Lights Be Burning

content: Hymn writer Philip Bliss and his wife Lucy went home to heaven together in a train accident just after Christmas in eighteen seventy six. Among his belongings was a new hymn, I Will Sing of My Redeemer. His friend James McGranahan set it to music, and the song Bliss never got to sing has been sung by millions since.
reference: I Will Sing of My Redeemer

content: For years, Away in a Manger was called Luther's Cradle Hymn, and many believed Martin Luther wrote it for his children. But hymn scholars have found it actually first appeared in America in the eighteen eighties. Whoever wrote it, generations of children have fallen asleep singing, the little Lord Jesus, asleep on the hay.

Phillips Brooks, a Philadelphia pastor, visited Bethlehem at Christmastime in eighteen sixty five. A few years later he wrote O Little Town of Bethlehem for the children of his Sunday school. His organist, Lewis Redner, said the melody came to him in the middle of the night, just before it was needed. A night gift for a night carol.

Edmund Sears, a Massachusetts pastor, wrote It Came Upon the Midnight Clear in eighteen forty nine. It is one of the few carols that speaks more of the angels' song of peace than of the manger itself. In a weary world, the song still says, rest beside the weary road, and hear the angels sing.
reference: It Came Upon the Midnight Clear

content: Martin Rinkart was a pastor in the walled town of Eilenburg, Germany, during the long and terrible Thirty Years War, when sickness swept the crowded town. Through all that sorrow he wrote Now Thank We All Our God. Gratitude that rises out of hard years is gratitude that lasts.
reference: Now Thank We All Our God

content: In eighteen thirty three, a young English clergyman named John Henry Newman was sailing home from Italy, weak from fever and homesick. His ship sat becalmed for a week in the Strait of Bonifacio. There he wrote Lead, Kindly Light. The night is dark, and I am far from home. Lead Thou me on. One step enough for me.

William Whiting of Winchester, England, wrote Eternal Father, Strong to Save in eighteen sixty. It became known as the Navy Hymn and is sung for sailors and all who travel the seas. For those in peril on the sea, and for everyone who feels adrift tonight, the eternal Father is strong to save.

Sweet Hour of Prayer is credited to William Walford, a blind English preacher. A visiting minister, Thomas Salmon, wrote down the words as Walford recited them, and they were published in a New York newspaper in eighteen forty five. A blind man saw clearly the comfort of time spent with God.

In eighteen seventy seven, Mary Lathbury wrote Day Is Dying in the West for evening vesper services at Chautauqua Lake in New York. As the sun went down over the water, people sang, holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts. It is still a perfect hymn for the close of day.
reference: Day Is Dying in the West

content: That same summer of eighteen seventy seven at Chautauqua, Mary Lathbury also wrote Break Thou the Bread of Life, for Bible study by the lake. She pictured Jesus breaking bread beside the sea and asked Him to break the bread of His Word for us. He is still feeding hungry hearts.
reference: Break Thou the Bread of Life

content: John Keble, an English clergyman and poet, published a beloved book of poems called The Christian Year in eighteen twenty seven. One evening poem became the hymn Sun of My Soul, Thou Savior Dear. It is not night if Thou be near. That is a line worth falling asleep on.

John Ellerton wrote The Day Thou Gavest, Lord, Is Ended in eighteen seventy. It pictures the church around the world praying in turn as the earth rolls on, so that the voice of prayer is never silent. Even now, while you are awake in the night, believers on the other side of the world are praying.
reference: The Day Thou Gavest, Lord, Is Ended

content: Bishop Thomas Ken wrote an evening hymn for the boys of Winchester College to sing in their rooms at night. One line asks God to teach me to live, that I may dread the grave as little as my bed. In Christ, even the last sleep holds no terror. It is only a bed, and morning comes.
reference: All Praise to Thee, My God, This Night

content: Lina Sandell of Sweden watched her beloved father fall overboard and drown in eighteen fifty eight. In the years that followed she poured her grief and faith into hymns, including Day by Day, written in eighteen sixty five. Day by day, and with each passing moment, strength I find to meet my trials here.

According to the traditional account, pastor John Fawcett had accepted a call to a large London church, and his wagons were loaded. But his poor country flock in Yorkshire wept so that he stayed. He wrote Blest Be the Tie That Binds, published in seventeen eighty two. Christian love is a tie worth keeping.
reference: Blest Be the Tie That Binds

content: Dudley Tyng, a young preacher, was badly injured in an accident on his farm in eighteen fifty eight. Before he died he sent a message to his fellow ministers, tell them to stand up for Jesus. His friend George Duffield turned those words into the hymn Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus.
reference: Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus

content: A French parish priest in eighteen forty seven asked a local wine merchant and poet, Placide Cappeau, to write a Christmas poem. Composer Adolphe Adam set it to music, and later an American, John Sullivan Dwight, translated it into English. We know it as O Holy Night. Fall on your knees.

Johann Sebastian Bach often wrote the letters S D G at the end of his music, for Soli Deo Gloria, glory to God alone. At the top of many scores he wrote J J, Jesus, help. Help at the beginning, glory at the end. That is not a bad pattern for any day of our lives.
